versions.summary: New routing guide for AI assistants pointed at the pattern set: pick the app shape, check which supporting patterns are triggered, and see what each guide contains before opening it.
changes: The seven pattern guides and their seven project prompts total about 353 KB. An assistant given the folder reads the first two or three guides, finds enough to start building, and stops. What it misses is never the app-shape guide -- it is the cross-cutting supporting patterns, because nothing in a build request announces that they apply

That is the expensive failure, because all three supporting patterns constrain the data model and none of what they constrain can be retrofitted: permission granularity needs the permissible unit to be a securable object from the first row, archive provenance columns and the Archives manifest cannot be backfilled, and a published contract has to be agreed before a consumer depends on it

The index is four ordered steps -- pick exactly one app shape, check the cross-cutting triggers, read the prompt rather than only the guide, and respect the Fixed/Default labels -- followed by a per-document section naming what only that guide settles and where to jump within it

A symptom-to-document table routes common failures and questions straight to a section: an .aspx that downloads instead of running, an undefined _spPageContextInfo, a 403 on a write, queries past 5,000 items, users who must not see each other's rows, a design that would create hundreds of lists, restored rows showing the wrong author

Carries the two known misreadings the Fixed/Default rule exists to prevent, so they are corrected at the entry point rather than after the fact: the shell's illustrative ~15 KB is not a hard limit, and 'sensitive data' is three different questions -- the platform can store confidential data, which is what the permissions pattern is for
Published as a Start Here card above the pattern cards on the hub, and wired into the repository through a new root CLAUDE.md and README.md so an assistant reads it before browsing the folder

versions.summary: Deploying into the site's default “Documents” library is now explicitly not recommended — apps get a dedicated library named for the app.
changes: The deployment requirement said to use “any regular document library (the default Documents, or a dedicated one)”, which read as an endorsement of the path of least resistance. It now calls for a dedicated library named for the app, with the default Documents library marked not recommended

Three reasons are given, because “it technically works” was winning the argument. Documents is the default target of the Add button, of Teams file uploads and of OneDrive sync, so an app deployed there shares a namespace with arbitrary user content: the deploy script's cleanup sweep can delete someone's spreadsheet, the Design or Full Control grant ends up covering the site's general file store rather than the app, and nobody browsing the library can tell which files are load-bearing

Updated everywhere the old advice appeared rather than in one place: the Requirements step, the Upload Order first step, the “two rules worth stating outright” bullet, the Add-PnPFile example that used -Folder 'Documents', and the Quick Reference row
The project prompt gained the same rule in its deployment section, which had said nothing about which library to use

deploy/examples/Deploy-MyApp.Example.ps1 defaulted -LibraryName to 'Documents', which was the strongest endorsement of the old guidance. It now defaults to a library named for the app, and its parameter help carries the one-time New-PnPList command — the script assumes the library exists rather than creating it

versions.summary: Fixes the Add and Customize Pages permission table, which had been rendering as literal pipe characters.
changes: The table listing which permission levels include Add and Customize Pages was indented three spaces as a continuation of the numbered step above it. The hub renderer only recognises a table when the line starts at column 0 (it tests line.charAt(0) === '|'), so every row fell through to the paragraph branch and readers saw the raw markdown — pipes, separator row and all — exactly where the guide explains why a shell uploaded without Design or Full Control downloads instead of running
De-indented to column 0; no wording changed. The constraint is now recorded with the renderer's other known limits so the next person does not re-indent it for tidiness and break it again

versions.summary: Split the fused 'no backend server, database, or external API' rule, and documented the premium-connector gate that made the old external-API advice unusable.
changes: 'Do not add a backend server, database, or external API' is now three rules, because they have three different answers and the strictest reading was winning. No backend server or separate hosting (fixed, it is the platform's premise). No app-owned database outside SharePoint (fixed — but reading data that already lives in SQL Server via Packaged Python is supported and always was). Consuming an external API is ALLOWED; what is fixed is where the call is made from

New 'Getting External API Data Into SharePoint' section with a routing table. The only fixed rule is that a credentialed call never happens in the browser, since a browser reads everything the page reads. Everything else is a Default chosen on licensing and uptime

Documented that Power Automate's generic HTTP action is a PREMIUM connector. The guide had listed 'call external REST APIs' as a flow capability without that caveat, so the advice quietly failed for anyone without a premium or per-flow licence — which is the default state for citizen developers here

Named the companion Packaged Python app as the workhorse route rather than a fallback: no premium licence, real Python for parsing and transformation, and it runs as a named person so rows it writes stay attributable. The seam is a SharePoint list, so the browser app never knows the API exists and the ingestion route can change later without touching it

The two 'self-service enablement page' links were relative (script-enablement.aspx), which resolved inside the pattern library. The enablement app now lives in its own script-enablement library, so both had been dead — they are now absolute URLs to the real page

Cross-links the new Cross-Application Communication pattern: the 'honest cost' of one site per app now hands off to a published contract instead of ending on the trade-off, the supporting-pattern line names it alongside Permissions and Storage, and the Power Automate section notes that when the caller is another EUDA app a flow is one of four shapes and usually not the first. The project prompt gains a matching 'do not read another application's internal lists' rule under What NOT to Build
The deploy script is renamed Deploy-SampleLibrary.ps1, matching the library it targets; the guide's command examples and library references follow it

versions.summary: Points at the new Cross-Application Communication pattern from the two places this guide raises the problem and then leaves it open.
changes: The 'honest cost' of one site per app — cross-app rollups get harder — used to end on the trade-off, which left 'read the other app's lists directly' as the reader's obvious next move. It now hands off to a published contract, and the supporting-pattern line beside it names Cross-Application Communication alongside Permissions and Storage

The Power Automate section notes that when the caller is another EUDA app rather than this app's own UI, a flow is one of four integration shapes and usually not the first to reach for — a SharePoint list carries the request with an audit trail and no bearer-secret URL to protect

The project prompt gains a matching rule under What NOT to Build: do not read another EUDA application's internal lists, even though SharePoint allows it — that is a dependency its owner does not know exists. Read only what that app published in its contract, and ask for CROSS_APP_COMMUNICATION_PROMPT.md before designing an integration
No other guidance changed; the shell is untouched, so this ships as a _data/-only update

versions.summary: Enabling a site is self-service now, not a help desk ticket — and the guide finally shows what a deploy script looks like.
changes: Custom-script enablement no longer says 'open a help desk ticket'. A vetted site owner opens their own 24-hour window in seconds, from the enablement page or from their deploy script, holding no admin rights at any point. The old wait was hours, and days over a weekend, which is long enough that people redesigned apps to avoid a shell change they could now make in seconds

Access is granted per site, once: register the site on the enablement page and an EUDA admin approves with one click. Several people can each hold a grant for the same site and enable it independently

New 'Deploying With a Script' section — the guide previously described manual uploads only, which is how shells get uploaded before their _data/ assets and how unchanged .aspx files get re-uploaded outside the window and lose their executable flag. Shows the shape of a deploy script: sign in as yourself, read the remote inventory first, enable only when a shell actually changed, upload _data/ deepest-first with shells last

New 'Opening the Window From Your Deploy Script' section with the self-service call, plus the three failure modes to expect (Denied, timed out, and window-open-but-still-downloading, which is the separate Design or Full Control requirement)

Why a script is permitted to enable a site at all, since it explains the whole trust model: SharePoint stamps Author on the request item and no client can set it, and the service re-checks (Author, SiteUrl) against an admin-curated grants list before flipping anything. The function key in the config is anti-DoS, not authorization — the same model as a Power Automate SAS URL

Sharing a document library between two apps is now a stated hazard: a cleanup sweep that deletes everything absent from the local source will delete the other app. The platform deploy script gained -PreservePaths, and its own default protects the self-service enablement app that now shares the `Sample Sites` library

Self-service is now the platform deploy script's DEFAULT way to open the window — euda-sample is registered with the enablement service, so a full deploy including a shell upload needs no admin rights at any step. -TenantAdminEnablement falls back to Connect-SPOService for a site that holds no grant. When the enablement queue lives on the site being deployed to, the existing connection is reused rather than prompting for a second sign-in

Two runnable examples added to the platform repo: deploy/examples/Enable-CustomScriptWindow.ps1 (paste-in helper) and deploy/examples/Deploy-MyApp.Example.ps1 (a complete minimal deploy script for one app)

versions.summary: Rules split into Fixed and Default, and two guidance defects fixed: the shell has no size limit, and "sensitive" was collapsing three different things.
changes: The shell size figure is no longer stated as a threshold anywhere it can be mistaken for one. The rule is behavioural — would this code ever change in order to add a feature? — and the guide now says plainly that THERE IS NO SIZE LIMIT on the shell, that 6-8 KB is what reference shells happen to weigh, and that ~15 KB is a smell to investigate rather than a budget or a ceiling. The Quick Reference row no longer quotes a number at all. v1.4 already tried to fix this by rewording; it kept the figure in the same sentence and readers kept pattern-matching on it

'Never put sensitive data in JavaScript' is replaced by three separately-stated rules, because collapsing them led people to believe the platform cannot hold confidential business data. SECRETS (anything granting access: keys, connection strings, tokens, flow URLs) are Fixed — a browser reads everything the page reads. CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS DATA (salaries, deal terms, HR records) is supported and is what the platform is for; the ACL protects it, not the UI. REGULATED DATA (PHI, payment card, export-controlled) is a governance boundary owned by IT — a conversation to start, not a permanent no

'Do not use React, Vue, or Angular' restated as the consequence of the actual fixed constraint, which is no build step. A no-build ES module loaded from _data/ does not break the rule; it is still not the default, and the decision gets recorded

Every guide and prompt now carries the Fixed/Default legend under its version header, and every prompt section is labelled (fixed) or (default). Fixed means deviation breaks the platform, its security model, its audit trail, or a protocol guarantee; Default means the right answer absent a specific reason — a judgement call, not a rule to obey

Prompts gained a 'How to read this prompt' preamble instructing Claude to propose the alternative and get agreement rather than silently deviating from a default — and, explicitly, never to tell the user that something a default merely discourages is impossible

Departing from a default now has a stated protocol: name it, say what makes this case different and what you give up, and record it in the app's README. If a Fixed rule is the obstacle, stop and escalate instead of working around it

versions.summary: Siting is now part of designing an app: one site per app, because a site's Owners group is the administrator list of everything inside it.
changes: New 'Where the App Lives: One Site Per App' section, opening 'Designing Your Application' — siting comes before schema. A site's Owners group holds Full Control, which includes Manage Permissions, so the site's owners administer every app in it; two apps in one site share an administrator list and no setting undoes that

Secondary reasons documented: capacity ceilings (2,000 lists and libraries, and each list's scope budget) stop being shared, storage and growth become legible, the 24-hour custom-script window is scoped to one app, sharing settings are per site, and decommission is a single delete instead of orphaned lists nobody dares remove

Conventions: communication site rather than team site unless an M365 group is genuinely needed, a visible naming convention (euda-<app-name>), a hub site to link sites without merging permissions, and a site registry list on the hub naming each app, its owners, purpose, and last-reviewed date

The honest cost is stated rather than glossed: cross-site rollups fall back to search, which is security-trimmed but index-lagged, so two things that must query each other row by row are one app in one site
Deployment requirements now cross-reference the siting decision — the enablement window is per site, which is one of the reasons not to share one. Requirement list renumbered accordingly
Quick reference gains a row for where to put a new app, and points access control and audit trail at the Permissions & Auditing pattern and sizing/archiving at Storage Shape & Lifecycle

versions.summary: Hardening from a consuming app on a shared site: deploys no longer clobber runtime-written config, enablement is inferred instead of switched, and the module manifest is validated before upload.
changes: Seed-only files are now a deploy-script parameter (-SeedOnlyFiles) instead of a hardcoded one-app array, and are exempt from the stale-file cleanup sweep — a remote-only seed is live data, not garbage. The guide documents the rule: if the app can write it, the deploy must not

Custom-script enablement is inferred from whether any .aspx actually needs uploading, so a _data/-only deploy needs no tenant-admin sign-in; -ForceEnablement overrides. Requires connecting and reading the remote inventory before the enablement step

Deploy-time pre-flight validates every manifest.json: valid JSON, non-empty module list, every named module present on disk, and FALLBACK_MODULES in the sibling app.js matching exactly. These fail at runtime, not deploy time, so the script aborts before shipping a broken app

Provisioning guidance: prefix provisioned lists with the app name through a single getListName() helper, and set the prefix before provisioning — changing it later strands the existing lists and their data rather than renaming them

Indexes and versioning must be applied at provisioning while the list is empty: an index added after 5,000 items will not take, and versioning enabled after writes begin has no history for them. Both shown as REST MERGE calls, run after field creation

New 'Writing List Items' section: fetch ListItemEntityTypeFullName for __metadata.type rather than guessing it (and cache it), a FieldTypeKind/__metadata correspondence table, and person columns taking a numeric <Field>Id from /_api/web/ensureuser
Corrected the paging guidance to follow the ready-made d.__next URL with a page cap, rather than reconstructing a $skiptoken query
Fixed an error in the project prompt's field-type comment, which listed 4 as Number; FieldTypeKind 4 is DateTime and Number is 9

versions.summary: Shell guidance is now a content rule, not a byte budget — plus a documented pattern for adding JS modules without ever redeploying the shell.
changes: Replaced the 'shell under 15KB' figure with a content rule: the shell holds boot logic only (asset loading, canonical helpers, loading/error UI) and no feature code or application state. Size is framed as a symptom — past ~15 KB, logic has leaked in — not as a ceiling to spend

Moved the rationale up to where the guidance first appears: content-scanner surface, plus the operational asymmetry (.aspx edits need a custom-script window and Design/Full Control; _data/ files need only Contribute)

Added 'Adding Modules Without Redeploying the Shell': a manifest.json listing modules in load order and a loader at the top of app.js that fetches each via $value, wraps it in a Blob, and appends a script tag — the same mechanism the shell already uses, so no eval() and no CDN. Includes the round-trip and fallback-list caveats
New shared helpers belong in a companion platform.js in _data/, not in the ticket-gated shell
'Updating Your Application' strengthened: no update should require changing the shell; if one appears to, the shell is holding logic that belongs in _data/
Updated the hello-world reference app and the repo manifest to state the same rule — both still described the shell by its byte size
Prompted by a consuming repo that hardened the 15KB guideline into an invented '< 12 KB' limit (its shells measure 7,151 and 6,529 bytes) and planned a help desk ticket it did not need

versions.summary: Concrete procedure for enabling browser-side Microsoft Graph: register the exact page URL as a SPA redirect URI on the shared registration.
changes: Replaced the 'browser Graph is unavailable until IT acts' guidance with a step-by-step enablement path: give IT the exact .aspx page URL (Entra matches redirect URIs exactly — no wildcards), IT adds it under the Single-page application platform, set MSAL redirectUri to match
Noted which Graph scopes are already consented (Mail.Read, Calendars.Read, Tasks.Read, People.Read, User.ReadBasic.All) and that Group.Read.All is not (Planner plan-name resolution)
Updated both the pattern guide and the project prompt

versions.summary: Editorial pass — tightened the prose for concision; no changes to guidance, code, or values.
changes: Ruthless-editor pass over the explanatory prose: cut padding, hedging, and redundancy. Code blocks, value tables, API scopes, endpoints, and error codes are unchanged

versions.summary: Correctness fixes: self-contained helper definitions, identity example, Graph token guidance, and a write-concurrency caveat.
changes: Canonical spPath/spFetch (and writeHeaders) helper definitions added to the project prompt — previously used throughout the snippets but never defined
Identity fallback now selects Id alongside Title/LoginName, and the 'my items' filter example uses the fetched id instead of _spPageContextInfo.userId (which is undefined in document-library ASPX)
Removed the 'app service account' wording from the flow-URL storage rule — the platform has no service accounts; restricted lists are readable to the app's users

Rewrote Graph guidance: SP.UserProfiles GetMyProperties is the no-token path; legacy SP.OAuth.Token/Acquire does not issue Graph tokens for custom pages; browser Graph requires msal-browser against the shared EUDA registration once IT adds a SPA redirect URI, with Power Automate as the fallback
Added a concurrency caveat to the IF-MATCH: * update/delete examples, cross-referencing the Worker Pool pattern's etag-conditioned writes

versions.summary: Initial release of the SharePoint App Pattern.
changes: Shell + Data pattern: lightweight .aspx shell loads CSS and HTML from a companion _data/ folder via the SharePoint REST $value endpoint
Identity resolution via /_api/web/currentUser with graceful fallback to _spPageContextInfo when available
Site URL derivation from window.location with _spPageContextInfo bonus when present
Write operations using a fresh digest fetched from /_api/contextinfo on every call
Full REST API CRUD against SharePoint lists with OData filtering, sorting, and $skiptoken pagination
List auto-provisioning: detects missing list via HTTP 404, creates list and custom fields on demand
JSON file data source pattern: fetch static data from _data/ folder via $value, parse client-side
Microsoft Graph integration for user profile and photo via /me endpoint
Power Automate HTTP trigger integration with URLs stored in a restricted AppConfig list
Hello World reference application demonstrating all patterns across Dashboard, Messages, Metrics, and About tabs

versions.summary: Rules split into Fixed and Default.
changes: The self-contained sandbox constraints are Fixed because the runtime enforces them; artifact type, styling, portability conventions, and handoff readiness are Default

Every guide and prompt now carries the Fixed/Default legend under its version header, and every prompt section is labelled (fixed) or (default). Fixed means deviation breaks the platform, its security model, its audit trail, or a protocol guarantee; Default means the right answer absent a specific reason — a judgement call, not a rule to obey

Prompts gained a 'How to read this prompt' preamble instructing Claude to propose the alternative and get agreement rather than silently deviating from a default — and, explicitly, never to tell the user that something a default merely discourages is impossible

Departing from a default now has a stated protocol: name it, say what makes this case different and what you give up, and record it in the app's README. If a Fixed rule is the obstacle, stop and escalate instead of working around it

versions.summary: Editorial pass — tightened the prose for concision; no changes to guidance, code, or values.
changes: Ruthless-editor pass over the explanatory prose: cut padding, hedging, and redundancy. Code blocks, artifact-type details, and the constraint tables are unchanged

versions.summary: Initial release of the Claude Artifacts development pattern.
changes: Artifact types and selection guidance: HTML, React, SVG, Mermaid, code, and markdown
Prompt patterns for generating production-quality artifacts
Iterative refinement workflow — describe, preview, refine in conversation
Tailwind CSS and inline style conventions for portable artifacts
Data embedding patterns for self-contained artifacts with no external dependencies
Handoff pattern: converting a Claude artifact prototype into a deployable SharePoint App Pattern application
Limitations reference: sandbox restrictions, no SharePoint API access, stateless between conversations

versions.summary: Apps can offer their own updates. The user is asked, the app stages the new app.py, and launch.cmd swaps it and restarts — replacing the email-attachment distribution this platform was actually running on.
changes: MIGRATION: the canonical launch.cmd changed, and app.py and launch.cmd must move together. An old launcher paired with a new app.py means the app exits 10, the launcher ignores it, and the app just closes with no update and no error. Redeploy both files to every app folder

New staged-update block, fixed and copied verbatim, offering a published release at startup: it prints the version, date, and notes, asks for an affirmative keystroke (no default-yes, no timeout), downloads the new app.py, verifies the sha256 published in version.json, and writes it to app.py.staged before exiting with code 10

launch.cmd gained an update tail: on exit code 10 it moves app.py to app.py.bak, moves the staged file into place, and restarts. EUDA_UPDATED bounds it to one swap per launch. The tail ships in every app whether or not the app updates — an app without the block never exits 10

The app never executes or imports what it downloads. Bytes land in a file, the process exits, and the launcher starts a fresh one from disk — mechanically identical to a person copying the file. That is the line the security carve-out is drawn on

Security rule amended: 'no runtime code download or execution' now names eval, compile, and import alongside exec, and states that downloaded bytes never become live code in the running process, with no exception. The staged updater is carved out as a canonical block the builder copies, explicitly 'not yours to write' — a hand-written fetch-and-run stays a defect even when it resembles the blessed one

The check runs pre-Streamlit, in the bootstrap branch, so sys.exit propagates normally and no server, browser tab, or session state exists yet to discard. Pattern B and Pattern C use the identical block

Cold token cache means skip the check: a freshly copied folder is current by definition, and the check must never be the thing that opens a sign-in browser. Every other failure path — offline, 403, malformed manifest, checksum mismatch, unwritable folder — also returns and runs the current version

The download URL is pinned to compiled-in site constants and never built from version.json's url field, so a tampered manifest cannot redirect the payload. Version comparison is ordered, so a rewritten manifest cannot push a pool backwards to an older release

New release library ACL requirements: break inheritance on the library, Owners Edit and everyone else Read (a communication site ships Members with Edit), keep Owners small and named in the app README, external sharing off, version history on. Write access to that library is now equivalent to code execution on every consumer's machine, and external sharing on it would make the updater an automated outside-Contoso distribution channel

version.json gained a sha256 field. It is not publisher authentication — manifest and payload share one ACL — but it closes the check-to-download window, catches corruption, and leaves an audit record of which bytes were published when
Distribution and versioning is default and opt-in: a single-user app has no release library and should leave the block out, keeping the blast radius proportional to the benefit

Fixed a latent defect found during the rewrite: all five sample launch.cmd files were saved LF despite the pattern requiring CRLF, which makes goto :label unreliable. Rewrote them as CRLF and added a .gitattributes rule, since the update restart depends on goto :run

versions.summary: Rules split into Fixed and Default, and the PII prohibition corrected — it read as "this platform cannot store a person's name".
changes: 'No PII or PHI in local files' corrected to 'no REGULATED data in local files'. Lumping PII with PHI made the rule unusable: names, email addresses, employee IDs, and org data appear in nearly every app on this platform. Ordinary personal and confidential business data is explicitly in scope — treat it as Internal, keep it under %LOCALAPPDATA% — while PHI, payment card data, and export-controlled material still escalate
The prompt now says outright never to tell a user this tier cannot store ordinary personal or confidential data

Stack and runtime choices stay Fixed, which is the point of the split: PEP 723 and uv, Streamlit for Pattern C, the approved library list, the canonical launch.cmd, and the security rules are binding. What became Default is the design surface — which library for a given job, the UI, the distribution channel

Every guide and prompt now carries the Fixed/Default legend under its version header, and every prompt section is labelled (fixed) or (default). Fixed means deviation breaks the platform, its security model, its audit trail, or a protocol guarantee; Default means the right answer absent a specific reason — a judgement call, not a rule to obey

Prompts gained a 'How to read this prompt' preamble instructing Claude to propose the alternative and get agreement rather than silently deviating from a default — and, explicitly, never to tell the user that something a default merely discourages is impossible

Departing from a default now has a stated protocol: name it, say what makes this case different and what you give up, and record it in the app's README. If a Fixed rule is the obstacle, stop and escalate instead of working around it

versions.summary: End-user polish for Pattern C, from a consuming app: the bootstrap silences two developer-facing Streamlit prompts, the launcher says how to stop the app, and every app ships a HOW-TO-RUN.md.
changes: First-run hygiene block now sets STREAMLIT_SERVER_FILE_WATCHER_TYPE=none. The watcher hot-reloads source while a developer edits it and has nothing to watch in a released app, but leaving it on greets every end user with 'install the Watchdog module' plus an xcode-select --install instruction. Documented why adding watchdog to the PEP 723 dependencies is the wrong fix: a native-component package on every operator machine for a feature that cannot fire in production

First-run hygiene block now writes the Streamlit skills-nudge marker, dismissing the in-app 'Help agents write better apps / Install the official Streamlit skills' dialog. There is no config option for it — the marker its own 'Don't show again' button writes is the only supported switch — so the block calls write_nudge_dismissed_marker() with a direct marker-file fallback, both arms wrapped so a failure cannot block startup

The matching terminal message is a separate code path gated on logger.hideWelcomeMessage, not the marker. Guidance is to leave it: hideWelcomeMessage also suppresses the URL: http://localhost:8501 line, and an app cannot reliably reprint that — get_option('server.port') read before launch ignores STREAMLIT_SERVER_PORT and config.toml, and pinning the port in sys.argv would break Streamlit's own fallback to the next free port

New 'The Launcher Says How to Stop the App' section: a Pattern C app keeps running after the browser tab closes and nothing said so. Canonical colour_supported() and print_banner() added to the project prompt, gating ANSI on NO_COLOR/FORCE_COLOR, isatty(), and the Windows ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING call, all stdlib; banner text is ASCII-only because cmd.exe's legacy code page turns box-drawing characters into mojibake

HOW-TO-RUN.md is now part of the project layout and the release folder. README.md is an owner-and-reviewer document; the colleague who was sent a folder needs a different page — launch.cmd on Windows and the slow first run, brew install uv plus uv run app.py on Mac, how to stop it, what to have in hand, and a table of likely errors
Updated the repo manifest's packaged-python app folder layout to match
Prompted by feedback from the Claude Custom Spend Limit Reset app, which built against v1.4 and had to apply all four of these outside the canonical block

versions.summary: Editorial pass — tightened the prose for concision; no changes to guidance, code, or values.
changes: Ruthless-editor pass over the explanatory prose: cut padding, hedging, and redundancy. The canonical launch.cmd, PEP 723 metadata, approved-library table, registration IDs, and all code blocks are unchanged

versions.summary: Confirmed the shared app registration is consented for the SharePoint list path (a typical app needs nothing from IT); recommend a blank communication site as the release channel.
changes: Verified with a live conditional write (the worker pool race proof) that the shared 'Contoso EUDA Applications' registration is already consented for the SharePoint list read/write path and common Graph reads (profile, mail, calendar, presence)
Documented that a typical app therefore needs nothing from IT to start; IT is involved only for a delegated scope beyond the consented set
Recommend creating a blank Communication site (not a Team site) as the team release channel — broadcast-shaped, no M365 group/Teams overhead — with a direct link to the SharePoint create-site flow

versions.summary: SharePoint-first data storage, the shared EUDA app registration, and team distribution via a SharePoint release channel.
changes: SharePoint Lists are now the preferred store for app-owned data; SQL Server is positioned for querying data that already lives there, not for new app storage — with an httpx + Bearer-token list-access example

Documented the shared IT-owned 'Contoso EUDA Applications' Entra registration (client <your-entra-client-id>, tenant <your-tenant-id>, http://localhost redirect); real IDs baked into the Graph and SharePoint REST code samples in both the pattern and the project prompt
Clarified that app releases never touch Entra — only requesting a not-yet-consented delegated scope involves IT (a one-time grant per scope, not per release)
Added team-distribution guidance: a SharePoint site as the release channel with a version.json and a non-blocking startup version check; pairs with the Worker Pool pattern
Clarified the Pattern B/C lettering: Pattern A is the browser-based SharePoint App Pattern, not something missing from this guide

versions.summary: Streamlit first-run hygiene added to the canonical Pattern C bootstrap.
changes: The self-relaunch bootstrap now pre-seeds ~/.streamlit/credentials.toml so end users never see Streamlit's 'Welcome / Email:' prompt on first run
Usage-stats telemetry disabled (STREAMLIT_BROWSER_GATHER_USAGE_STATS=false)
Toolbar set to viewer mode (STREAMLIT_CLIENT_TOOLBAR_MODE=viewer) — hides the Deploy button (Streamlit Community Cloud is not approved hosting) and developer menu items
Applied to the existing Pattern C samples (sql-schema-explorer, data-explorer) and to the project prompt's canonical snippet

versions.summary: Initial release of the Packaged Python pattern.
changes: Single-file applications: one app.py with PEP 723 inline script metadata, run via uv — recipients install nothing but uv itself
Two app shapes: Pattern B (script — automations, reports, ETL) and Pattern C (Streamlit UI at localhost)
Python 3.12 runtime pinned via requires-python; uv provisions the interpreter and an isolated environment automatically
Approved stack with one library per job: httpx, mssql-python, sqlalchemy (local SQLite), pandas, openpyxl, msgraph-sdk, pydantic, keyring, tenacity
SQL Server access as the signed-in user via mssql-python — Entra ActiveDirectoryInteractive or Windows integrated (Trusted_Connection) on on-prem servers; no passwords, no service accounts
DB2 data reached exclusively through the IT-managed SQL Server linked server (OPENQUERY pass-through) — no IBM drivers
Microsoft Graph integration via msgraph-sdk and InteractiveBrowserCredential with persistent, DPAPI-protected token cache
Canonical launch.cmd that installs uv automatically when missing (winget first, official installer fallback — user-space, no admin), so recipients have zero prerequisites
Self-bootstrapping Streamlit pattern so the same launcher works for both app shapes
Security rules: no hardcoded secrets (keyring only), parameterized SQL only, localhost-only UI binding, writes restricted to %LOCALAPPDATA%
Explicit escalation boundaries: unattended execution, inbound network exposure, and regulated data are out of scope for the citizen tier

changes: The worker should carry the staged-update block: a mixed-version pool is the exact failure mode it prevents, and convergence costs each participant one keystroke
The dashboard's 'a newer version is available' banner stays, now scoped to its real job — a release published while a worker is already running, which the startup check cannot catch
Write access to the release library is equivalent to code execution on every participant's machine; the ACL requirements are called out and cross-referenced to the Packaged Python guidance

versions.summary: Scheduled and background automation with no server — a Packaged Python worker on each participant's machine, coordinated through SharePoint lists.
changes: Composition pattern: a Packaged Python Pattern C worker app + SharePoint App Pattern conventions for coordination lists and a read-only status page
Jobs as data: recurring jobs live in a Schedules list (JobType, ParametersJson, IntervalMinutes, NextRunDue, Enabled); job code lives in an owner-reviewed catalog in the worker

Atomic claiming via SharePoint optimistic concurrency: MERGE with If-Match etag — exactly one concurrent claimer gets 204, all others get 412; no lock files, no leases, nothing to clean up after a crash

Every run logged to a JobRuns list (status, runBy, timings, output/error) — the audit trail is a native SharePoint list

versions.summary: Rules split into Fixed and Default, and two operational preferences demoted from prohibitions.
changes: 'NEVER put an individual on an ACL' and 'NEVER break inheritance by hand in the UI' were listed among the security invariants. Neither is one: both cost maintenance rather than safety. They moved to a new 'Operational defaults' section that states what deviating costs and when it is a reasonable call — a single long-lived unit with one named reviewer, or a unit whose permissions will never change

What remains Fixed is what is genuinely load-bearing: do not filter by role in client code and call it access control, do not let a list decide access instead of the ACL, do not store an admin role, do not cache a security-trimmed result for other users, every write happens as the acting user, and do not break inheritance in a runtime loop over existing data

'Choosing the securable level' relabelled Default with the Microsoft limits it quotes marked as external facts rather than house rules. The siting and setup-page guidance in section 9 is Default, and now states when the alternative is defensible instead of forbidding it

Every guide and prompt now carries the Fixed/Default legend under its version header, and every prompt section is labelled (fixed) or (default). versions.summary: Supporting pattern: use SharePoint site, list, library, folder, and file permissions as the application authorization layer, and get an audit trail without writing one.
changes: The permissible-unit rule: before designing lists or columns, name the smallest thing two people might need different access to, and make it its own securable object. Granularity cannot be retrofitted without a data migration, so it is a day-one decision — a deal in an M&A tracker is a folder, not a row

The securable ladder (site / list / folder / item) with the service limits that pick the level: 5,000 unique scopes per list recommended (50,000 supported), 2,000 lists and libraries per site collection, and no breaking or restoring inheritance once a container passes 100,000 items. Folder-per-unit is the default choice

Security trimming is the query filter: issue the plain GET and SharePoint returns only what the caller may read. Includes the composition move — the set of objects a user can read is itself a fact about that user, so an org hierarchy can be reconstructed from ACLs alone with no hierarchy stored anywhere

Groups are the join table: one group per permissible unit, that group is the sole ACL entry, and every access change is a membership write. Covers SharePoint vs Entra group choice and why removals, not adds, are the failure mode

Site owners are automatically the application administrators. Full Control includes Manage Permissions, so derive the admin flag from /_api/web/effectivebasepermissions (ManageWeb = Low & 0x40000000) instead of storing a role list — effective permissions catch ownership arriving through nested Entra groups, which currentUser/groups misses

The boundary that follows: you cannot durably hide data from a site owner or a site collection administrator, and ReadSecurity/WriteSecurity do not apply to them. If data must be invisible to the owners it needs a separate site — which makes siting the real security decision

Seven design shapes with worked REST: folder-per-unit (M&A tracker), list-per-unit (region split), file-per-principal ACL-as-graph (HR manager portal), segregation of duties via a separate approvals list, restricted configuration, read-mostly reference data, and personal drafts via ReadSecurity/WriteSecurity = 2 (per-creator privacy at zero unique scopes)

provisionUnit() as a fixed sequence — create, break inheritance, grant the group, then read the ACL back and assert it. The read-back is mandatory: breakroleinheritance(copyRoleAssignments=false) does not leave an empty ACL, it leaves the calling user with Full Control

Auditing from what SharePoint already stamps: Author/Editor, versioning (enabled at provisioning — history cannot be backfilled), the recycle bin for deletions, GetChanges for activity feeds, and role assignments for who can see it now. Who changed the permissions lives in Purview, which citizen apps cannot read, so an app that grants access must write its own provenance rows

Framed the platform no-service-account rule as an audit rule: every write happens as the acting user, or the trail collapses to one name. Notes the Power Automate caveat — a flow runs as its connection owner, not the requester

Section 9 gives the permissions-specific reason for three operational practices documented elsewhere: one site per app (SharePoint App Pattern) because two apps in one site share an administrator list; provisionUnit() inside a setup page (Storage Shape & Lifecycle) so the ACL that exists is the one somebody reviewed and a second site reproduces it exactly; and two admin-page panels nothing else surfaces — unique scopes against the 5,000 recommendation, and the access report comparing live ACLs to the grants list

Anti-pattern table, gotchas (Limited Access, sharing links creating unstated scopes, untrimmed ItemCount, short pages that still have a __next, search index lag), and a thirteen-step design checklist to work through before the first list is created

versions.summary: Rules split into Fixed and Default — correcting a first release that labelled most of its design guidance (fixed).
changes: Mechanism selection, the hybrid shape, sprawl control, setup pages, admin pages, and archive granularity are Default. v1.0 marked most of these (fixed), which was wrong: they are the judgement calls the pattern exists to inform

'NEVER propose a design that provisions hundreds of lists' sat inside the section labelled the judgement call. It now says to stop and make the case out loud with the ceiling arithmetic, and acknowledges the real exception — a list carries per-row versioning and safe concurrent writes a file cannot

What stays Fixed is data safety: verify-then-delete ordering, capturing Author/Created/Editor/Modified into the archive envelope, archive immutability, archived records staying read-only, the Original* provenance columns, and the disclosure of what does not survive a rehydration round trip
The setup-page section now allows that a short manual checklist is defensible for a single site with two lists and no permissions work — said explicitly rather than drifted into

versions.summary: Supporting pattern: how many objects the storage layer creates, which mechanism can carry them, and what happens to data when it gets old.
changes: Shape follows count and lifetime: two questions decide the mechanism — how many units at three years, and does a unit's content need server-side querying, safe concurrent writes, or per-row history. A decision table maps count and answer to list-per-unit, folder-per-unit, file-per-unit, or the hybrid

Named the failure mode directly: a design that would provision hundreds of lists is a folder of files in disguise. Symptoms listed (identical schemas, dozens of rows each, no cross-list querying, provisioning as part of unit creation). Same per-unit ACL and same one scope, without the schema overhead or the 2,000-list ceiling
A list-vs-file cost table. Concurrency is usually the deciding factor: files have no transaction safety, so anything two people can edit at once must be a list

The hybrid shape — a shared index list of non-sensitive metadata plus an ACL'd payload file per unit — giving cross-unit dashboards and per-unit privacy at once, and a clean answer to the permissions guide's "absence is ambiguous" problem. One hard rule: nothing sensitive in the index

Sprawl control: unit-count budgets displayed on the admin page, no speculative provisioning, naming that sorts, group accumulation against the 10,000-per-site-collection ceiling, and a scheduled orphan sweep that reports and never auto-fixes (with a table of what it looks for)

Hot/cold/gone tiering and the archive contract: a self-describing immutable archive envelope (schema version, source, unit, period, row count, checksum, provenance, columns, rows) and an Archives manifest list that is security-trimmed, so "which archives may I load?" is answered per user

The archiver must capture Author, Created, Editor, and Modified INSIDE the file — once the source rows are deleted it is the only surviving record of who did what. Called out as the most expensive mistake available in the pattern

Verify, then delete — never delete, then write. Fixed order with a REST sketch: page the source, build the envelope, write the file, re-read it from SharePoint, verify row count and checksum, write the manifest row, only then delete. A crash anywhere leaves either untouched source data or a complete archive plus the source data

Archive-aware reads: hot by default, explicit opt-in, read-only by construction with no edit affordances, filtered to State === Archived so rehydrated rows do not appear twice, and merged for display only

Dehydration and rehydration: rehydration copies and never moves, whole units only, capped against the 5,000-item view threshold, idempotent, and re-dehydration writes a new file and supersedes the old rather than overwriting

The audit trap, with a what-survives table: rehydrated rows are new list items, so SharePoint stamps Author/Editor with the restorer. Original* provenance columns must be provisioned at setup or the original history is lost; per-row version history, item IDs, per-row permissions, and attachments do not survive unless explicitly handled

Setup is a page, not a procedure — eight requirements (idempotent, previews before applying, correctly ordered, provisions the lifecycle machinery and the permissions, permission-gated with a plain-English message, self-verifying, schema-version-stamped, kept after go-live). Moved here from the Permissions pattern, which now cross-references it

Administrative pages, with a ten-panel table (provisioning state, unit count vs budget, scope budget, threshold headroom, storage and growth, archive inventory, orphan sweep, access report, config in effect, provenance) and five rules — derived never authoritative, gate and degrade, be honest about the viewer's lens, preview and confirm destructive actions, and link to tenant tooling rather than approximating it

Retention, ownership, and decommission decided while the lists are still empty; anti-pattern table; eleven-step design checklist; and an escalation boundary that separates an operational archive from Purview retention, legal hold, and defensible disposal

changes: v1.0 named the self-service custom-script enablement service as the platform's live instance of the request-queue shape but could not link it — the app was mid-move between libraries and every candidate URL was dead. Both references are now links to the real page
The hub pointer in the version header uses the current library URL; v1.0 shipped with it already corrected, and the other guides were caught up separately
No guidance changed; _data/-only update, no shell touched

versions.summary: How one app asks another for data or work — SharePoint lists standing in for an API, behind a published contract that says what may be depended on.
changes: First release. Answers the cost the SharePoint App Pattern names but leaves open: one site per app makes cross-app rollups harder, and every team's workaround so far has been to read the other app's internal lists directly — which works until the day the producer renames a column and finds out a consumer exists

The published boundary (fixed): an app's lists are private, and other apps read only what it has deliberately published. Enforced by three mechanics because SharePoint enforces none of it — a 'Pub' naming segment so the boundary shows in site contents, a broken-inheritance group sized for the consuming audience, and the contract file that makes it accountable. Publish a projection, never the internal schema

The communication contract: <app>_data/contract.json at a well-known path, carrying every publication's fields, types, plain-English SEMANTICS, freshness promise, audience, retention and version. Machine-readable so a consumer can check it at startup, human-readable so a reviewer can read it. Registered in the site registry with a ContractUrl column — the registry is an index, the file is the truth

'consumes' is half the contract and the half that gets skipped. Every app declaring its dependencies in the same field of the same file at the same path turns 'who breaks if I change this?' from an email to everyone into a sweep. Each dependency carries degradesTo — what the app does when it is missing, stale, or an unknown version. An integration with no answer to that is not finished

Four shapes, chosen deliberately: published dataset (the default — a self-describing JSON snapshot, seed-only in the deploy script), published list, event feed (append-only, consumers hold their own cursors and never write back), and request queue. Power Automate remains the escape hatch for genuinely synchronous calls, with its trigger URL treated as the bearer secret it is

The request queue is a list that behaves like an API: a state machine of Pending / Claimed / Succeeded / Failed / Expired / Rejected, one writer per transition, response written back on the same item, correlation id as the idempotency key so a repeat returns the first result instead of doing the work twice

Claiming a request is the Worker Pool's conditional write, unchanged and for the same reason: MERGE with If-Match on the etag captured at read — one caller gets 204, the rest get 412, and 412 is the system working. The fencing guard and the code-catalog rule (Operation is a key into reviewed functions; nothing from a payload becomes code or a path) carry over intact

Identity and authorization (fixed), the pattern's most expensive mistake: the provider executes as itself, so a request queue hands every writer the provider's reach and is a privilege boundary. The requester is the Author SharePoint stamped, never a RequestedBy field, and authorization is re-checked at processing time against a list the provider controls — so a grant revoked after submission is seen. This generalizes the platform's own self-service enablement service, which has run exactly this way since 2026-08-25

Compatibility rules (fixed): additive only within a version; consumers are tolerant readers; a breaking change is a new version published alongside the old with a deprecation date and a registry sweep for who to tell. Never repurpose a field — changing what a name means while the name and type stay put yields confidently wrong data for months, where a deletion would have failed loudly on the first read. SchemaVersion is stamped on the row, not only in the contract, because records outlive it

Two verifications every implementation ships, the counterpart to the Worker Pool's race proof: a contract check at startup that turns a future breaking change into a specific message naming app, publication and versions rather than silent bad data, and a replay proof showing a duplicated event or correlation id leaves consumer state identical

Cross-site mechanics stated once so they stop being rediscovered: one tenant means one origin and no CORS work, a write into another site needs a digest from THAT web, security trimming still applies per user so a narrowly-granted publication looks broken to some people and not others, and search rolls up across sites but lags the index by minutes to hours — discovery and reporting only, never a workflow's read path

Freshness is displayed, not hidden: any UI showing another app's data shows its source and age, degrades to the declared fallback with a message naming the other app, and polls on the contract's interval with jitter. There are no cross-app transactions — one app owns the truth and the other reconciles
